[latex]\lt[/latex][latex]\lt[/latex] binds tighter than [latex]\&[/latex], so the test is [latex](num\ll i)\ \&\ (1\ll15)[/latex]: after shifting left by i, it checks bit 15. For i = 0 to 15 this reads bits 15, 14, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 0, i.e. it prints num in binary from the most significant bit.

Answer: It prints binary equivalent of num

questions.solution:
The inner "int i = 10" is a new variable inside the loop body that hides the loop counter. It is created as 10 every iteration, printed, and its ++ does not affect the outer i. The loop runs 5 times.

Output: 10 10 10 10 10

Answer: 10 10 10 10 10

questions.text:
What does the following C-statement declare?
 int (*f) (int * );
questions.solution:
Read from the name outwards: (*f) means f is a pointer; (int *) means to a function taking an int pointer; the leading int is its return type.

Answer: A pointer to a function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns an integer

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: A function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns an integer
A function that takes an integer as argument and returns an integer pointer
A pointer to a function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns an integer
A function that takes an integer pointer as argument and returns a function pointer

questions.solution:
swap receives copies of x and y (call by value) and exchanges only the copies; x and y in the caller are unchanged. Passing [latex]\&[/latex]x, [latex]\&[/latex]y would not even match int parameters.

Answer: swap(x,y) cannot be used as the parameters are passed by value

questions.solution:
square([latex]\&[/latex]number, [latex]\&[/latex]number) calls the two-argument version, where x and y both point to number. Reading *x first gives 30, then --(*y) makes number 29:
*x = 30 [latex]\times[/latex] 29 = 870

(Strictly, mixing a read and a modification of the same variable in one expression has unspecified order; the keyed answer uses left-to-right evaluation.)

Answer: 870
